Wielun Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Wieluń, Poland

Not demolished. Wieluń, granted town rights in 1283, recorded its first Jews in 1537, though the De Non Tolerandis Judaeis privilege pushed early settlement to nearby villages; the community developed significantly only after Poland's partitions. By the 1890s, 2,502 (37.8%) grew to 43.7% (4,818) by 1921 and 33.4% (5,247) by 1938, with Jews holding prominent postwar civic roles. A spring 1941 ghetto's August 1942 liquidation deported nearly all 10,000 Jews to Chełmno, sparing only 922 able-bodied workers sent to the Łódź Ghetto; of about 80 postwar returnees, seven were murdered, prompting the rest to leave. This cemetery, probably established around 1850, included a funeral house and caretaker's residence. Germans carried out mass executions here during WWII, killing several hundred Jews, including a public execution of ten people in winter 1942; ghetto victims' bodies were also interred at the site, with the last recorded burial in 1942. Postwar, the grounds were reforested; the 1980s saw cleanup efforts add a commemorative obelisk.
